preamble: Depalatalization of the voiceless palatal stop [c] to the alveolar or dental stop [t] fronts the tongue contact and removes the palatal articulation. The clearest documented case is Egyptian: the Old Egyptian palatal ṯ /c/ (itself from palatalized *k) frequently merged with t from the end of the Old Kingdom onward, although many lexemes kept ṯ and later developed an affricate instead.

examples.note: Wiktionary lists the alternative writings tn and Late Egyptian twn.
In Late Egyptian the t-forms became the normal spellings and the pronoun became common gender.

examples.to: Middle Egyptian /ˈtuʀwuw/, Sahidic Coptic ⲧⲏⲩ (tēu), Bohairic ⲑⲏⲟⲩ (thēou)
examples.note: The Coptic reflexes show a dental stop where Old Egyptian had the palatal; the homographic verb ṯꜣw 'to steal' instead developed an affricate (Coptic ϫⲓⲟⲩⲉ).
The palatal had become a dental stop by Middle Egyptian; Bohairic ⲛⲟⲩϯ (nouti) likewise has t.

Proto-Tapajoara changed coda *c to *t; Timbíra has j in the same words (Parkatêjê kəj 'axe'). Forms in Nikulin's Macro-Jê alphabet: ñ = [ɲ], j = [j ~ ʒ], c = [tʃ ~ tɕ ~ ts ~ c], ĵ = [dʒ ~ ɟ], ə̂ = [ɘ ~ ɤ], y = [ɨ ~ ɯ], ê/ô = close-mid [e]/[o], ṭʰ = aspirated alveolar stop, mb/nd = post-oralized nasals; a final ’ marks a coda without echo vowel, X // Y gives phrase-medial // prepausal allomorphs.

sources: Allen, J. P. (2013). The Ancient Egyptian Language: An Historical Study. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139506090
Nikulin, A. (2020). Proto-Macro-Jê: um estudo reconstrutivo. https://repositorio.unb.br/handle/10482/38893
